---
title: "Missing values"
subtitle: "Bounced emails, uncoded replies and missing covariates"
bibliography: [../references.bib, ../references-new.bib]
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
# The estimator of the case study, for spec_frame()
source("../R/_tools.R")

# readr rather than datawizard::data_read(), which returns some empty cells as ""
housing <- readr::read_csv("../data/housing_emails.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

The values that a data file does not hold, and the effect of each way of handling them on an estimate, form the subject of this module of the [companion curriculum](index.qmd). In the field experiment on which the Housing and racial bias case study rests, described in full on the [background page](../background.qmd), the original authors emailed public housing authorities across the United States from names meant to indicate a white, a Black or a Hispanic applicant and found that replies to the Hispanic names opened with the sender's name less often [@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect]. The original authors' public file is unusually complete for a social-science dataset, yet it lacks three kinds of information, each missing for a different reason and each entering the analysis at a different point. Every number on the page is computed from the course file `data/housing_emails.csv` when the page is built, and the construction of that file is followed step by step in the [module on building the analysis file](data-management.qmd).

## 1. Three kinds of missing information {#sec-kinds}

```{r}
#| label: counts
#| include: false
ref <- spec_frame(housing, comparison = "white", population = "replies", uncoded = "drop")
replies_wh <- housing |>
  datawizard::data_filter(reply == 1, group %in% c("white", "hispanic")) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(hisp = as.integer(group == "hispanic"))
n_sent <- nrow(housing)
n_bounced <- sum(is.na(housing$reply))
n_replies <- sum(housing$reply %in% 1)
n_uncoded <- sum(housing$reply %in% 1 & is.na(housing$named))
n_uncoded_wh <- sum(is.na(replies_wh$named))
n_thirds <- sum(is.na(housing$pop_third))
n_thirds_replies <- sum(is.na(housing$pop_third) & housing$reply %in% 1)
n_assess <- sum(is.na(housing$assessment_third))
```

@tbl-kinds presents the three kinds, together with the third in which each housing authority falls on the assessment score of the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). No specification on the curve uses this assessment third, but since it is missing far more often than anything else in the file, it illustrates what the choices examined in section 5 can do when much is at stake. The last column counts the rows affected by each kind of missing information in the reference specification of the course, that is, among the coded replies to white and Hispanic names.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-kinds
#| tbl-cap: "The kinds of missing information in the Housing data: how often each is missing in the file, when it arises in the experiment, and how many of the coded replies to white and Hispanic names, the rows of the reference specification, it affects. Source: `data/housing_emails.csv`."
#| echo: false
tibble::tibble(
  `Missing information` = c("Reply status of an email that bounced", "Greeting code of a reply",
                            "Community thirds of an authority", "HUD assessment third of an authority"),
  `In the file` = c(paste(n_bounced, "of", format(n_sent, big.mark = ","), "emails"),
                    paste(n_uncoded, "of", n_replies, "replies"),
                    paste(n_thirds, "of", format(n_sent, big.mark = ","), "emails"),
                    paste(n_assess, "of", format(n_sent, big.mark = ","), "emails")),
  `When it arises` = c("before any official read the email", "after the reply arrived",
                       "recorded about the authority, before the emails", "recorded about the authority, before the emails"),
  `Reference rows` = c("none: no bounced email is a reply",
                       paste(n_uncoded_wh, "replies left out of", nrow(replies_wh)),
                       paste(sum(is.na(ref$pop_third)), "of", nrow(ref)),
                       paste(sum(is.na(ref$assessment_third)), "of", nrow(ref)))
) |>
  tinytable::tt()
```

A fourth absence, of a different kind, runs through the whole file. The `r sum(housing$reply %in% 0)` delivered emails that drew no reply have no greeting at all, since a greeting exists only where a reply exists. The missing greeting of these emails is neither a value that was recorded and then lost nor one that a coder could not read, but an outcome that never came into being, and the problem that it raises, that of comparing greetings only among the emails that drew a reply, is a problem of design rather than of missing data. This problem is taken up in the [module on audit experiments](experiments.qmd#sec-posttreatment) and the [module on causal graphs](dags.qmd#sec-collider), and is left aside on this page.

## 2. Why a value is missing {#sec-mechanisms}

The consequences of a missing value for an estimate depend on why the value is missing, and the vocabulary for describing the reasons goes back to @Rubin1976InferenceMissingData. In the review by @Little1992RegressionMissingXs, values are missing completely at random (MCAR) when the chance that a value is missing does not depend on any value in the data, observed or not, and missing at random (MAR) when it depends only on values that are observed (p. 1229). Values missing for reasons connected with what is missing, such as an income left blank because it is high, are missing not at random. Under MCAR the cases with complete data form a random subsample of all the cases, and an analysis of the complete cases alone thus loses precision but nothing else: "If the data are MCAR, listwise deletion will not introduce any bias into parameter estimates" [@Allison2009MissingData, p. 75]. Listwise deletion, the default of almost every statistical program, drops every case with a missing value in any variable of a model.

An experiment raises a further question, not asked by the three categories, namely whether the treatment could have changed whether a value is missing. @ZhaoDing2024AdjustNotAdjust make the point for covariates recorded before treatment: "the missingness indicators act as fully observed pretreatment covariates as long as missingness is not affected by the treatment" (abstract). A missingness indicator is a 0/1 variable recording, for each case, whether a value is missing, and the point of the quoted sentence is that such an indicator, when settled before the treatment was assigned, is information about the cases like any other, which random assignment balances between the groups whether or not the values themselves are known. This is why @tbl-kinds records, in its last column but one, when each kind of missing information arises. Since the community thirds and the assessment third describe the authority and its community, from values measured by the census and by HUD, the name cannot have changed whether the thirds are missing. A bounce, likewise, is settled when the email fails to arrive, before any official could react to the name. The greeting codes, however, are the exception, since the five uncoded replies were written by officials who had read the name, and whether a reply could be coded may in principle depend on what the name led the official to write.

## 3. Bounced emails {#sec-bounced}

Of the `r format(n_sent, big.mark = ",")` emails sent, `r n_bounced` bounced, and these emails, which never reached an official, carry no reply status, since the original authors' codebook records the reply as missing "if email bounced back due to email issue". The chunk below counts the bounced emails by the group of the name and by whether the address was hard to find.

```{r}
#| label: bounced
housing |>
  datawizard::data_modify(bounced = as.integer(is.na(reply))) |>
  datawizard::data_summary(emails = n(), bounced = sum(bounced), share = 100 * mean(bounced), by = "group")

housing |>
  datawizard::data_modify(bounced = as.integer(is.na(reply))) |>
  datawizard::data_summary(emails = n(), bounced = sum(bounced), share = 100 * mean(bounced), by = "hard_email")

stats::chisq.test(table(housing$group, is.na(housing$reply)))$p.value
```

```{r}
#| label: bounced-numbers
#| include: false
bounce_by <- housing |>
  datawizard::data_modify(bounced = as.integer(is.na(reply))) |>
  datawizard::data_summary(emails = n(), bounced = sum(bounced), share = 100 * mean(bounced), by = "group")
bounce_p <- stats::chisq.test(table(housing$group, is.na(housing$reply)))$p.value
# With fewer than ten bounces for each name, the p-value of the test across the
# six names, each its own sending account, is simulated rather than read from
# the chi-square distribution
set.seed(20261105)
bounce_name_p <- stats::chisq.test(table(housing$name, is.na(housing$reply)), simulate.p.value = TRUE, B = 9999)$p.value
# The twin of the menu page: every delivered email to a white or Hispanic name,
# an uncoded reply counted as not named, against every email sent, a bounced
# email counted as unanswered
delivered_twin <- spec_frame(housing, comparison = "white", population = "all", uncoded = "not_named")
all_sent <- housing |>
  datawizard::data_filter(group %in% c("white", "hispanic")) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(hisp = as.integer(group == "hispanic"),
                          y = dplyr::if_else(reply %in% 1, dplyr::coalesce(named, 0), 0))
gap_delivered <- 100 * stats::coef(stats::lm(y ~ hisp, data = delivered_twin))[["hisp"]]
gap_sent <- 100 * stats::coef(stats::lm(y ~ hisp, data = all_sent))[["hisp"]]
share_of <- bounce_by$share[match(c("white", "black", "hispanic"), bounce_by$group)]
```

The bounces are few and spread across the groups, at `r insight::format_value(share_of[1], digits = 1)`% of the emails with white names, `r insight::format_value(share_of[2], digits = 1)`% with Black names and `r insight::format_value(share_of[3], digits = 1)`% with Hispanic names, and a $\chi^2$ test finds no more difference between the groups than chance would produce (`r insight::format_p(bounce_p, stars = FALSE)`). For the name to have caused a bounce, a mail server would have had to refuse a message because of its sender. The counts by group give no reason to suspect such a refusal, but the counts by name are uneven, all the bounces among the white names having come from Emily and none from Brett, with none from Tyrone either. Chance would rarely produce such a spread across the six names (a $\chi^2$ test across the six names, with its p-value simulated because the counts are small, gives p = `r formatC(bounce_name_p, format = "f", digits = 3)`), and the sending account may thus have played a part. A bounced email is therefore arguably best read as an email to which the treatment was never delivered, for reasons that no official could have influenced. Leaving the bounced emails out, as every specification on the curve does, keeps the comparison among the delivered emails nearly as random as the assignment of the names made it.

The alternative, counting a bounced email as one that went unanswered, matters only when all emails are counted, since a bounced email is never a reply. Among all delivered emails to white and Hispanic names, with the uncoded replies counted as not named, the gap in greetings by name is `r insight::format_value(gap_delivered, digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` points. Counting the bounced emails as unanswered moves the gap to `r insight::format_value(gap_sent, digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` points, a change that is small but produced by broken addresses rather than by officials, which is why the [specification menu](../menu.qmd#level-measurement) excludes the bounced emails from the curve.

## 4. Replies without a greeting code {#sec-uncoded}

The original authors coded the greeting of every reply but `r n_uncoded`, and the file does not indicate why these five replies were left uncoded.

```{r}
#| label: uncoded
housing |>
  datawizard::data_filter(reply == 1, is.na(named)) |>
  datawizard::data_select(c("email_id", "name", "group", "hard_email", "reply24"))
```

Three of the five uncoded replies went to white or Hispanic names, two to Emily and one to Santiago, and only these three can move the comparison stated in the claim. The specification menu offers two ways of handling the uncoded replies, the first of which, leaving them out, is what a model does by default and what four of the five analysts in the SCORE robustness study [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness] did. The second, counting the uncoded replies as replies that did not open with the name, is a defensible reading, since a reply in which the coders found no greeting probably did not begin with one, and analyst 25N5D made that choice, without stating it, by keeping these replies in the counts of emails. Because the uncoded replies arose after the officials had read the name, neither option can rely on random assignment, and the safest check is one that assumes nothing about why the codes are missing. Such a check is provided by the two extreme codings, one counting all three replies as named when the name was Hispanic and as not named when it was white, which moves the gap as far towards zero as these replies can move it, and the other doing the reverse.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-uncoded
#| tbl-cap: "The gap in greetings by name between Hispanic and white names among the replies, under four codings of the three uncoded replies to these names: left out, counted as not named, and the two extreme codings. Differences in proportions with HC2 standard errors. Source: `data/housing_emails.csv`."
codings <- list(
  `left out` = datawizard::data_filter(replies_wh, !is.na(named)),
  `not named` = datawizard::data_modify(replies_wh, named = dplyr::coalesce(named, 0)),
  `named if Hispanic, not if white` = datawizard::data_modify(replies_wh, named = dplyr::coalesce(named, hisp)),
  `named if white, not if Hispanic` = datawizard::data_modify(replies_wh, named = dplyr::coalesce(named, 1 - hisp))
)
# dplyr inside the lambda, because datawizard does not see the arguments of a function
uncoded_gaps <- purrr::imap(codings, \(d, coding) {
  stats::lm(named ~ hisp, data = d) |>
    parameters::model_parameters(vcov = "HC2") |>
    dplyr::filter(Parameter == "hisp") |>
    dplyr::mutate(coding = coding, replies = nrow(d))
}) |>
  purrr::list_rbind()

uncoded_gaps |>
  datawizard::data_modify(gap = sub("^-", "−", sprintf("%.1f", 100 * Coefficient)),
                          se = sprintf("%.1f", 100 * SE)) |>
  datawizard::data_select(c(Coding = "coding", `Gap (points)` = "gap", SE = "se", Replies = "replies")) |>
  tinytable::tt() |>
  tinytable::style_tt(j = 2:4, align = "r")
```

Since the gap stays between `r insight::format_value(max(100 * uncoded_gaps$Coefficient), digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` and `r insight::format_value(min(100 * uncoded_gaps$Coefficient), digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` points under every coding, the uncoded replies cannot change the conclusion, whatever their true greetings were. Bounds of this kind are the first check to run whenever an outcome is missing for a few cases, because such bounds need no assumption about why the values are missing and settle the question when the cases are few. With more missing outcomes the bounds would widen until they conveyed nothing, and the analysis would then require an argument about why the outcomes are missing, the situation addressed for the emails without a reply by the [trimming bounds of the module on audit experiments](experiments.qmd#sec-posttreatment).

## 5. Missing covariates {#sec-covariates}

The adjusted specifications on the curve add to the model the hard-to-find address and the community thirds, covariates recorded before the emails went out. Since the names were assigned at random, no covariate is needed to remove bias, and the adjustment serves only to narrow the standard error, as the [module on audit experiments](experiments.qmd#sec-randomisation) explains. A covariate that is missing for some authorities therefore raises a narrower question than it would in an observational study, namely how to retain the precision offered by the covariate without changing the comparison. The literature offers four answers to that question, compared in the rest of this section on the case-study data.

**Complete cases.** `lm()` drops every row with a missing value in any variable of the model, as does the course estimator, and the specifications that adjust for the community thirds therefore rest on `r sum(!is.na(ref$pop_third))` of the `r nrow(ref)` coded replies in the reference comparison. @KingEtAl2001AnalyzingIncompletePolitical found that "approximately 94%" of the articles that they reviewed in political science used listwise deletion, "losing about one-third of their data, on average" (p. 49).

**Complete covariates.** An adjustment for the covariates observed for every authority, here the hard-to-find address alone, retains every row, and @ZhaoDing2024AdjustNotAdjust treat this adjustment as the baseline against which the other strategies are judged, since it is valid in a randomised experiment whatever the reason for the missing values.

**A category for the missing.** Each covariate with missing values receives one additional category, or a 0/1 indicator, marking the rows without it, and the model retains every row. @Allison2009MissingData describes the method, for a categorical predictor, as one "whereby an extra category is created to hold the cases with missing data", and rejects it for regression on observational data, since a proof by Jones shows that it "typically produces biased estimates of the regression coefficients, even if the data are MCAR" (p. 76). @ZhaoDing2024AdjustNotAdjust reach the opposite recommendation for randomised experiments, for the reason given in section 2, namely that when whether a covariate is missing was settled before the treatment, the indicator is a covariate recorded before treatment like any other, and adding it leaves the comparison of the experiment intact. In such experiments Zhao and Ding do not recommend the complete-case analysis, which estimates the effect among the complete cases and thus recovers the effect among all cases only if the two effects are the same (section 4.1).

**Multiple imputation.** Each missing value is replaced, several times over, by a draw from a model that predicts it from the other variables, the analysis is run on each completed dataset, and the results are combined by Rubin's rules, which add the variation between the completed datasets to the standard error. The mice package imputes variable by variable by chained equations, using by default a logit or a multinomial logit for a factor and predictive mean matching for a number [@BuurenGroothuis-Oudshoorn2011MiceMultivariateImputation, pp. 11, 22–23]. The authors of the package advise including in the imputation model "all variables that appear in the complete-data model, i.e., the model that will be applied to the data after imputation", the outcome included, since leaving these variables out "will tend to bias the results towards zero" (p. 22).

As the community thirds are missing for only `r sum(is.na(ref$pop_third))` coded replies, the four answers can differ only a little, and the chunk below fits the place adjustment used on the curve (the hard-to-find address and the thirds of population and poverty) both as complete cases and with a category for the missing.

```{r}
#| label: place
# The thirds as factors, and copies with a fourth level for the missing
frame <- ref |>
  datawizard::data_modify(.at = c("pop_third", "poverty_third", "assessment_third"),
                          .modify = \(x) factor(x, levels = c("lower", "middle", "top")))
frame_mi <- frame |>
  datawizard::data_modify(.at = c("pop_third", "poverty_third", "assessment_third"),
                          .modify = \(x) factor(dplyr::coalesce(as.character(x), "missing"),
                                                levels = c("lower", "middle", "top", "missing")))

place_fits <- list(
  `no adjustment, all replies` = stats::lm(y ~ hisp, data = frame),
  `no adjustment, complete cases` = stats::lm(y ~ hisp, data = datawizard::data_filter(frame, !is.na(pop_third))),
  `place set, complete cases` = stats::lm(y ~ hisp + hard_email + pop_third + poverty_third, data = frame),
  `place set, category for the missing` = stats::lm(y ~ hisp + hard_email + pop_third + poverty_third, data = frame_mi)
)
place <- purrr::imap(place_fits, \(fit, label) {
  parameters::model_parameters(fit, vcov = "HC2") |>
    dplyr::filter(Parameter == "hisp") |>
    dplyr::transmute(model = label, gap = 100 * Coefficient, se = 100 * SE, replies = stats::nobs(fit))
}) |>
  purrr::list_rbind()
place |> dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(c("gap", "se"), \(x) round(x, 2)))
```

The complete-case adjustment moves the gap from `r insight::format_value(place$gap[1], digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` to `r insight::format_value(place$gap[3], digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` points, and a comparison of the first three rows shows that part of this move comes from dropping the five replies, before any covariate enters, since the unadjusted gap among the complete cases is already `r insight::format_value(place$gap[2], digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` points. When a category for the missing is used instead, retaining every reply, the adjusted gap is `r insight::format_value(place$gap[4], digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` points. `lm()` reports one coefficient as not estimable in that model, because the same five replies lack both thirds, which makes a category for the missing in one third a duplicate of the category in the other, and R drops the duplicate.

The assessment third makes the difference between the answers visible, because it is missing for `r sum(is.na(frame$assessment_third))` of the `r nrow(frame)` coded replies, almost a third of the total. Nor is it missing completely at random, since the replies from authorities in the lower third of communities by population lack it far more often than the replies from authorities in the top third.

```{r}
#| label: assessment-pattern
frame |>
  datawizard::data_modify(assessment_missing = as.integer(is.na(assessment_third))) |>
  datawizard::data_summary(replies = n(), missing_share = 100 * mean(assessment_missing), by = "pop_third")

frame |>
  datawizard::data_modify(assessment_missing = as.integer(is.na(assessment_third))) |>
  datawizard::data_summary(named_share = 100 * mean(y), replies = n(), by = c("assessment_missing", "group"))
```

```{r}
#| label: assessment-gaps
#| include: false
by_missing <- frame |>
  datawizard::data_modify(assessment_missing = as.integer(is.na(assessment_third))) |>
  datawizard::data_summary(named_share = 100 * mean(y), by = c("assessment_missing", "group"))
# Hispanic minus white: the groups sort as hispanic, white
gap_complete <- by_missing |>
  datawizard::data_filter(assessment_missing == 0) |>
  datawizard::data_arrange("group") |>
  datawizard::data_extract("named_share") |>
  diff() * -1
gap_incomplete <- by_missing |>
  datawizard::data_filter(assessment_missing == 1) |>
  datawizard::data_arrange("group") |>
  datawizard::data_extract("named_share") |>
  diff() * -1
```

Among the replies from authorities with an assessment third, the gap between Hispanic and white names is `r insight::format_value(gap_complete, digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` points, against `r insight::format_value(gap_incomplete, digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` points among the replies from authorities without one. The difference may well be due to chance, since each group of replies is small, but the situation is exactly one in which a complete-case analysis changes what is estimated, because dropping the incomplete cases leaves the gap among the authorities that have an assessment score rather than the gap among all the authorities that replied. The chunk below fits the adjusted model under four ways of handling the missing scores, beside the unadjusted gap, the last two being the interacted regression with a category for the missing recommended by @ZhaoDing2024AdjustNotAdjust, fitted with `estimatr::lm_lin()`, and multiple imputation with mice, pooled with HC2 standard errors.

```{r}
#| label: assessment-fits
assess_fits <- list(
  `no adjustment, all replies` = stats::lm(y ~ hisp, data = frame),
  `no adjustment, complete cases` = stats::lm(y ~ hisp, data = datawizard::data_filter(frame, !is.na(assessment_third))),
  `assessment third, complete cases` = stats::lm(y ~ hisp + assessment_third, data = frame),
  `assessment third, category for the missing` = stats::lm(y ~ hisp + assessment_third, data = frame_mi)
)
assess <- purrr::imap(assess_fits, \(fit, label) {
  parameters::model_parameters(fit, vcov = "HC2") |>
    dplyr::filter(Parameter == "hisp") |>
    dplyr::transmute(model = label, gap = 100 * Coefficient, se = 100 * SE, replies = stats::nobs(fit))
}) |>
  purrr::list_rbind()

# The interacted regression of Zhao and Ding, with the covariate centred and
# interacted with the treatment, and HC2 errors
lin <- estimatr::lm_lin(y ~ hisp, covariates = ~ assessment_third, data = frame_mi, se_type = "HC2") |>
  estimatr::tidy() |>
  datawizard::data_filter(term == "hisp")

# Twenty imputations of every missing covariate from all the other columns,
# the outcome and the treatment included (van Buuren and Groothuis-Oudshoorn
# 2011, p. 22); each completed dataset fitted with HC2 errors and the results
# combined by Rubin's rules with mice::pool.scalar()
imputation_data <- frame |>
  datawizard::data_select(c("y", "hisp", "hard_email", "pop_third", "poverty_third", "assessment_third"))
imputed <- mice::mice(imputation_data, m = 20, seed = 20261105, printFlag = FALSE)
per_imputation <- purrr::map(seq_len(imputed$m), \(i) {
  stats::lm(y ~ hisp + assessment_third, data = mice::complete(imputed, i)) |>
    parameters::model_parameters(vcov = "HC2") |>
    dplyr::filter(Parameter == "hisp")
}) |>
  purrr::list_rbind()
pooled <- mice::pool.scalar(Q = per_imputation$Coefficient, U = per_imputation$SE^2,
                            n = nrow(imputation_data), k = 4)

assess <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  assess,
  tibble::tibble(model = c("interacted, category for the missing", "multiple imputation, 20 datasets"),
                 gap = 100 * c(lin$estimate, pooled$qbar), se = 100 * c(lin$std.error, sqrt(pooled$t)),
                 replies = nrow(frame))
)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-assessment
#| tbl-cap: "The gap in greetings by name between Hispanic and white names among the coded replies, adjusted for the HUD assessment third under four ways of handling its missing values, beside the unadjusted gap among all replies and among the complete cases. Linear probability models with HC2 standard errors; the imputations are combined by Rubin's rules. Source: `data/housing_emails.csv`."
#| echo: false
assess |>
  datawizard::data_modify(gap = sub("^-", "−", sprintf("%.1f", gap)), se = sprintf("%.1f", se)) |>
  datawizard::data_select(c(Model = "model", `Gap (points)` = "gap", SE = "se", Replies = "replies")) |>
  tinytable::tt() |>
  tinytable::style_tt(j = 2:4, align = "r")
```

Every strategy that retains all `r nrow(frame)` replies yields a gap close to the unadjusted `r insight::format_value(assess$gap[1], digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` points, from `r insight::format_value(max(assess$gap[c(4, 5, 6)]), digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` to `r insight::format_value(min(assess$gap[c(4, 5, 6)]), digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")`, with standard errors of about `r insight::format_value(mean(assess$se[c(1, 4, 5, 6)]), digits = 1)` points. The complete-case analysis, by contrast, yields `r insight::format_value(assess$gap[3], digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` points on `r assess$replies[3]` replies, with a larger standard error, and almost the whole of its departure is already present in the unadjusted gap among the same complete cases. While the adjustment itself appears to change little, dropping the authorities without a score changes the comparison and costs the precision that the adjustment was meant to buy.

Multiple imputation adds almost nothing here. The part of the variance in the gap attributable to the variation between the imputations, reported by mice as the fraction of missing information, is `r insight::format_value(pooled$fmi, digits = 3)`, because the name was assigned at random and thus carries no information about the missing scores, whatever these scores are. In an experiment the category for the missing yields the same answer without any model of the missing values, and it is on this ground that @ZhaoDing2024AdjustNotAdjust argue for preferring it. Imputation earns its place where the variable with missing values is itself the object of the analysis rather than an aid to precision. A comparison of the gap across the thirds of percent Hispanic, presented in the [subgroups module](subgroups.qmd), cannot give the replies without a third a category of their own, and an observational comparison, such as one among the officials who replied, has no random assignment to fall back on. In such analyses the observational case argued by @Allison2009MissingData and by @KingEtAl2001AnalyzingIncompletePolitical applies in full, and the plausibility of MAR, here a missing score explained by the size of the community and the other recorded columns, becomes the assumption on which the estimate depends.

## 6. Missing values on the curve {#sec-curve}

Each kind of missing information enters the specification curve of the case study in its own way. The bounced emails lie outside the experiment under every option, because no official read a bounced email. The handling of the uncoded replies is a decision on the menu, with these replies either left out or counted as not named, and the two extreme codings of section 4 show that no handling of the uncoded replies can change the conclusion. The community thirds are handled as complete cases, and the specifications adjusting for them therefore lose `r sum(is.na(ref$pop_third))` of the `r nrow(ref)` coded replies in the reference comparison. Part of the shift between the adjusted and the unadjusted specifications, as the [specification menu](../menu.qmd#level-estimation) notes, comes from the rows lost by the adjustment rather than from the adjustment itself. A declared analysis can name a different handling, such as a category for the missing, provided that the declaration names it before the model is run, since a choice made after the estimates are known is itself one of the forking paths discussed in the [multiverse module](multiverse.qmd).

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Fit the specification of the curve with the fullest adjustment (the hard-to-find address and the thirds of population, poverty, percent Black and percent Hispanic) as complete cases with `fit_spec(housing, adjust = "place_ethnic")`, then with a category for the missing in each third, and decide how much of the difference between the two comes from the five dropped replies. Then rerun the imputation with `m = 5` and two different seeds, and compare the pooled gaps and their standard errors with those in @tbl-assessment. Finally, write the sentence of a preregistration that states how your declared analysis handles each of the three kinds of missing information of @tbl-kinds.
:::

## Sources and further reading {#sec-sources}

The terms used in section 2 come from @Rubin1976InferenceMissingData, and @Little1992RegressionMissingXs reviews the methods for regression with missing covariates, while @Allison2009MissingData offers a short, clear introduction to listwise deletion, to the methods that replace a missing value with a guess, and to maximum likelihood and multiple imputation. The case for the missing-indicator method in randomised experiments, and against complete cases there, is made by @ZhaoDing2024AdjustNotAdjust, under assumptions about nothing but the random assignment. Multiple imputation in political science is presented by @KingEtAl2001AnalyzingIncompletePolitical, and the mice package is described by its authors [@BuurenGroothuis-Oudshoorn2011MiceMultivariateImputation]. The construction of the course file, together with the checks on its missing values, is documented in the [module on building the analysis file](data-management.qmd), and the counts for every column are given in the [codebook of the course file](../data/housing_emails_codebook.md).
